title: Does Math Achievement h’APP’en when iPads and Game-Based Learning are Incorporated into Fifth-Grade Mathematics Instruction?
venue: Journal of Information Technology Education: Research
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether adding iPads and game-based learning activities to elementary mathematics instruction improves student achievement. The author frames the problem as persistent weakness in mathematics performance and argues that mobile technologies may create more engaging and interactive learning experiences than traditional instruction.

The study used a nonequivalent groups pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design in two rural Virginia elementary schools. The sample included 104 fifth-grade students and two fifth-grade teachers. The experimental group used iPads as 1:1 devices during math class for one academic quarter, with activities such as game-based apps, online tutorials, presentations, and virtual manipulatives; the control group received regular instruction without daily iPad use. Student achievement was measured with a curriculum-aligned standardized math assessment administered before and after the intervention.

Results showed that both groups improved over time, but the difference in gain between the iPad group and the control group was negligible and not statistically significant. The author concludes that, in this implementation, iPad-supported math instruction did not produce measurable achievement benefits. The paper suggests possible reasons include the short duration, limited access to devices outside math class, pre-existing group differences at baseline, and the possibility that the assessment may not have captured broader 21st-century learning gains.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a quantitative quasi-experimental study with pretest-posttest comparison and a clearly described outcome measure, but it is not randomized and has important internal validity concerns (baseline nonequivalence, clustered classes, small sample, non-normality). It provides usable adjacent evidence, but credibility is below a strong RCT.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported impact on mathematics achievement was essentially null: both groups improved over time, but the iPad condition did not outperform control in any meaningful way. Any observed difference was trivial and not statistically significant.

interventions.use_case: 1:1 iPad-supported mathematics instruction in fifth grade, including daily use of educational apps, online video tutorials, review presentations, and interactive manipulatives during math class.
game-based learning applications used on iPads as a component of fifth-grade mathematics practice and reinforcement.
tablet-based mobile learning with iPads as portable 1:1 classroom devices for accessing math activities and digital instructional materials.

finding.finding_summary: In this quasi-experimental nonequivalent groups study of 104 fifth-grade students (iPad n=56, control n=48), iPad-supported mathematics instruction did not significantly improve achievement relative to the comparison group. Both groups improved from pretest to posttest (control: 55.58% to 62.25%; iPad: 61.05% to 67.79%), but the growth difference was only 0.07 percentage points and the repeated-measures ANOVA was not significant.
finding.measure: Scott Foresman-Addison Wesley fifth-grade mathematics Virginia SOL-aligned pretest and posttest scores (50-item multiple-choice assessment)
finding.std_deviation: control pretest SD=11.81; iPad pretest SD=15.7; control posttest SD=12.01; iPad posttest SD=15.92
